label: paragraph_title
text: SPLEEN AND TEMPER.

label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong, Wednesday, Sept. 8, 1926

label: text
text: Whatever case, Mr. Eugene Chen may have had against the British for the naval intervention at Canton has been completely spoiled by spleen and bad temper, which has led him to lose his nerve and descend to fabrications and insults unworthy of any man in his position. His is a sorry sered indeed, and simply shows that the present Canton regime lacks the first principles of statesmanship and diplomacy. Furthermore, it reveals what has all along been suspected—that the Canton Government will not candidly admit the lawlessness of the pickets' outrages nor their breaches of international treaties during the last fourteen months, against which it has been repeatedly warped.

label: text
text: Having failed to profit by the intervention of the small British naval party on the British wharves in Canton by repudiating the pickets entirely, the Canton Government has fallen into the trap of ranging itself on the side of the pickets. It can no longer sit on the fence and toy with the dictionary in an effort to convince outsiders of its sincerity in assisting to end the boycott. It has been forced openly to commend the weapon of the boycott and to threaten, reprisals by means of that same weapon which has led to all the present trouble and to the cleavage between the Governments of Canton and Hong Kong.

label: text
text: In descending to such scurrilous expressions as Britain's "gunboat policy" and the "rough-neck method of the sailor" the Canton Government has placed itself out-

label: text
text: with the pale of an ordinary controversy in a list. These phrases may seem courteous and dignified to Mr. Eugene Chen, but to nobody else. They deserve to be treated with that silent contempt which they so richly deserve. In the language of the ring he has "hit below the belt" and accordingly must be ruled out by the impartial umpire. He has lost the fight by foul methods and incidentally besmirched his own character.

label: text
text: At the time of writing the official reply of the British Consul-General has not reached us, but if the report cabled to one of our morning contemporaries may be taken as trustworthy, our representative in Canton seems to have given a Roland for an Oliver. He asks in laconic terms why, if China is not at war with Great Britain, is Hong Kong blockaded and British products classed as enemy goods? And, very pertinently, he adds that an explanation for this is necessary before the withdrawal of the British warships. The Canton Government, it is now clear, was hand in glove with the pickets and therefore a party to all the illegal outrages committed by the latter during the last fourteen months. Little wonder that it now whines and groans when it finds the occupation of the pickets on the river frontgone. Little wonder that it feels aggrieved that it should have been taught a salutary lesson on how to maintain law and order by a mere handful of British blue-jackets. The only pity is that that lesson was not administered to it long ago!

label: paragraph_title
text: Not Botany Bay.

label: text
text: Prominence having been given to the fact that deportees from other colonies, are sent here, Hong Kongites may think they have just cause for being indignant. "This is a fine state of affairs," writes a correspondent. "Is Hong Kong a second Botany Bay?" he asks. No, this little outpost of empire is by no means a convict settlement nor a repository for undesirables. By reason of its geographical position—its proximity to the homes of deportees from neighbouring colonies—Hong Kong is a sort of distributing centre. That a never ceasing campaign is waged to weed out bad characters is evident from the number of persons—of both sex—deported when a conviction is not feasible. Then there are those banished after a term in jail. Further there are the mendicants who are packed off to beg in their own cities. Not so long ago, the usual term of deportation was five years. It is rarely under ten now. So much for what is being done to rid the Colony of pests in our own midst. People with no fixed means of abode or other underworld "characters" of Singapore and other places are rounded up and repatriated. The Hong Kong authorities, being in closer touch, act as receiving agents and then send the deportees on to their respective destinations. Of the Chinese who come back under guard from the South, it should be stated that the majority are not Cantonese, in the strict sense of the term. Some are Hokloq from the Swatow district. Others may hail from Hainan Island. Then there are natives of Fukien province. On arrival in Hongkong, the deportees are marched up to Police Headquarters where fingerprints are taken. A special man who is trained for the job looks after the emigrants and supervises their departures from our shores.

label: paragraph_title
text: CORRESPONDENCE.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE Y.M.C.A. MEDICAL CAMPAIGN.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRAISEWORTHY EFFORT

label: text
text: [To the Editor of the "China Mill.] Sir, — The efforts of the Chinese Y.M.C.A. in attempting to inculente into the Chinese populace an elementary grounding in hygiene is indeed praiseworthy and if there were similar organisations capable of carrying on a campaign throughout the country a great reduction in the mortality figures, could be effected, as a large percentage of the deaths in China are avoidable.

label: text
text: In China, unhappy, effective sanitation is conspicuous by its absence and the conservation of infant life is something which has not yet been fully grasped by the Chinese. The result is that the rate of infant mortality in this country is abnormally high and much potential man-power is thus lost to the nation.

label: text
text: A case in point has been furnished in Shanghai where thousands have been attacked by the dread malady of cholera and a large percentage have succumbed to the disease.

label: text
text: The number of foreign cases of cholera, even in periods of the worst epidemic, as the “China Press” points out, is negligible. What is the reason for such a disparity between the Chinese and foreign cases? Why is it that foreigners, many of whom are alien to the climate of China, asks the same paper, contrive to survive the rigours of a severe summer whilst those indigenous to the soil and acclimatised to lqcal atmospheric conditions pay such a heavy toll whenever cholera rages in a particular area?

label: text
text: Is it not because the masses 'of the people refuse to adopt those elementary measures of' precaution, both as regards "food and drink, which are enjoined" on the foreigner and Chinese alike", but which only a slender proportion of the latter take seriously?

label: text
text: It is disheartening, to observe the pathetic faith which the majority of Chinese repose in quack doctors of the "kill or cure" order. As a rule he kills, in which case there is nothing to worry about, but if in other instances he contrives to cure his victim, it is not because of the proficiency shown, as the "China Press" points out, but in spite of him.

label: text
text: The work of the Chinese Y.M.C.A. in endeavouring to replace the faith of the masses in charlatanry by a grounding in the elementary laws of hygiene is a commendable one which will meet with the approval of all who have the best interests of the Chinese at heart.

label: paragraph_title
text: HEATING FOR SNAKI

label: paragraph_title
text: LUXURIOUS CAGES AT THE ZOO.

label: text
text: After prolonged research work, a wonderful system of heating, lighting, and stimulating has been arranged for the snakes and alligators in the London Zoo's new Republic House which will be ready next year.

label: text
text: Dark heat-rays and tonic light-rays are part of the scheme, and when a snake dies, in future, the Zoo will accept no excuse save that of senile decay, or, possibly, cunibalism by a third party.

label: text
text: The cages will be glimpses of nature with beautifully "modelled backgrounds designed by Miss Joan Procter, who created the water-pictures in the Zoo Aquarium. The alligators will sun themselves on shelving "Florida benches" fringed with water-plants, and tropical vegetation. You will see no flower-pots in the "snakes" and lizards' enclosures to shatter your illusions.

label: text
text: All these cages will show themselves as "brilliantly-lit" spectacles to visitors who themselves walk in a pleasant twilight.

label: text
text: Each reptile will be given exactly the right amount of electric heat. If 82 degrees is prescribed, a thermostat (heat regulator) will be set to that pbint, and the warmth will be shut off automatically if it is exceeded. The sandy floor will be heated, the water warmed, and the air-temperature controlled in the same way. The failure of a thermostat will report itself electrically in a control-room.

label: text
text: Zoo visitors will find the atmosphere in the new Reptile House no warmer than that outside the building, and the old reproach of stuffness will vanish.

label: paragraph_title
text: WELL KNOWN'SHANGHAI CHINESE.

label: text
text: It is with very deep regret that we have to record the death of Mr. Chu Pao-ann, which occurred at his residence in Shanghai at the ripe age of 79 years.

label: text
text: He is rightly called the veteran merchant of Shanghai, having been in business in Shanghai for more than 60 years. Born in 1847 in the city of Tinghai, Chekiang, Mr. Chu indeed had a most varied and interesting commercial life, serving as the head of many industrial enterprises.

label: text
text: As chairman of the Chinese General Chamber of Commerce, Shanghai he enjoyed the confidence of all Chinese and foreigners in the community on account of his spirit of public service and keen sense of justice.

label: text
text:
He also served as the Vice-chairman of the National Association of Chambers of Commerce. In Banking, he promoted the Commercein Bank of China, the Ningpo Commercial Bank, Ltd., the Cheklang Industrial Bank, Ltd. and the Chang Hwa Commercial and Sayings Bank. In insurance he was organiser of the Wah An Fire and Marine Insurance Co., Ltd., the Wah Sing Insurance Co., Ltd. and the China United Assurance Society Ltd.
In mining, Mr. Cha was directing the Lila Kiang and Chang Hsin Mining Companies. In electric

label: text
text: Mr. Willim H. Stayton, head of the Association Against the Prohibition Amendment, testified to his organisation's activities before the Senate investigation committee.

label: text
text: works, he had considerable interests in the Shanghai Nantao Tramway Co., Ltd., the Ting Hai Electric Construction Co. and "the Chousan Electric Co.

label: text
text: In navigation, Mr. Chu was director of the Chusan Steam Navigation Co., the Yung An Steamship Co., the Yung Lee Shipping Co. and the Chang Ho Navigation Co.

label: text
text: Besides these Mr. Chu organised the Lung Chang Paper Mill, the Ta Yu Factory, the Ta Tah Steamship Co., the Nantao Water Works, the Shanghai Cement Co., the Li Dah and Chung Hsin Flour Mills, the Shanghai Silk Manufacturing Co., the First Woollen Goods Factory, the Ho Hsin Iron Foundry, the Ho Fung Cotton Mill and others.

label: text
text: He was director of the "Sin Wan Pao," a leading Chinese daily newspaper. He was trustee for the Shanghai Commercial School, the College, the Ting Hai School, the Tung Chi Medical and Engineering Sheng Yi School in Tinghai and Yi Chi School of Ningpo. In philanthropic and public enterprises, he was director of the Union Club, the Chinese Red Cross Society, the Ningpo Guild, the Ting Hai Guild, the Door of Hope, the Kwang Yi, Jen Chi and Wei Chung Benevolent Institution, the Ningpo Hospital, the Kwang Chi Hospital, the Tung Chi Hospital, the Shanghai Summer Disease Hospital, the Woosung Quarantine Hospital, the Shanghai Kung Li Hospital, the Shanghai Orphanage, the Hsin Pu Pi Tang, the Pu Yi Industrial Home, the Anti-Kidnapping Society, the Tung Yi and Liengyl Philanthropic Institutes, the Bureau for the Cheap Sale of Rico and the International Famine Relief Committee.

label: text
text: Chu Pac-san was a man, who, apart from his outstanding ability in the world of commerce was a resident of Shanghai in the truest sense of the word. A man of engaging character and sterling worth his business preoccupations at no time prevented him from doing the best service possible in the community in which he lived, and foreigners as well as Chinese have occasion to be grateful for the fact that such a man of such excellent qualities could find the time he did to serve them in a manner which will always be associated with his name.—N. C. Daily News.

label: paragraph_title
text: BOULDER SMASH..

label: paragraph_title
text: WAS REPORT MADE 2 YEARS AGO?

label: text
text: UNIVERSITY COMPLAINT?

label: text
text: P.W.D. witnesses were questioned at the adjourned inquiry yesterday into the Pokfulam pumping house disaster as to whether their attention had been drawn to the danger from insecure boulders at that spot two years ago.

label: text
text: None of the witnesses in question had any recollection of any such report, they stated: if such had been made it would have been referred to the P.W.D. in the first instance and then probably direct to the Building Authority. The overseer in charge of the district would ultimately have been detailed off.

label: text
text: Mr. R. S. W. Paterson, engineer in the Building Ordinance Office, P.W.D., was questioned as to whether in the ordinary way such a report would have come to him. If it had been made two years ago, He stated that it probably would and in any case he would have been informed. If it had not come to him for action he would have handled it for filling purposes and either he or the overseer would have been deputed to the scene. He had no knowledge of any such report.

label: text
text: In reply to other questions witness said that he visited the scene on the morning of the disaster and climbed to the place where the rock hall come from. The ground was very sodden at that point but there was no evidence of a washout by water. Witness thought that many years ago the two boulders, one of which was still on the ledge from which the other had fallen, had formed one.

label: text
text: Mr. R. E. Lindsell, Coroner, said he had been informed that morning that Professor Earle, of the University of Hongkong, who was at present in Shanghai, had made a report of insecure boulders at the spot in question. He suggested that witness should communicate with Mr. Pearce, engineer of the P.W.D., telling him what he (the Coroner) had heard and ask him to come to the Court and make a statement.

label: text
text:
This was done and it was intim-
ated that Mr. Pearce was at Homq two years ago and therefore could not say if any report was made.

label: text
text: Mr. Paterson added that records had been searched and no trace of any such report could be found.

label: text
text: The inquiry was adjourned until September 19.

label: paragraph_title
text: GAS FATALITY

label: paragraph_title
text: JURY RECOMMEND USE OF MASKS.

label: text
text: ACCIDENTAL DEATH.

label: text
text: A recommendation that gas masks should be used was made at the further inquiry into the death of a coolie from the effects of gas poisoning while working at the Pedder Street nullah.

label: text
text: The inquiry was conducted by Major Willson at the Central Magistracy yesterday, assisted by a jury.

label: text
text: Mr. D. S. Edward, assistant engineer, P.W.D. deposed to having issued a warning to the contractors prior to the accident to use precautions when the leakage of gas was discovered. He handed in a copy of the regulations concerning work of this kind, and said that "contractors were notified of the regulations.

label: text
text:
The foreman of the jury said he understood that gas masks were used in such cases at Home. Witness said he had put forward the idea and some reflection had been cast on it, the question being raised of whether the coolies would understand the masks.
In reply to another question by the foreman, witness said the use of masks ensured safety but he thought some of the Chinese were not sufficiently intelligent to wear them. Major Willson commented that all recruits had to learn how to use masks.

label: text
text:
Witness added that gas masks were obtained from the military authorities and brought into use when the work was held up.
Commenting on the evidence, Major Willson said the man was discharged from hospital as cured, but there was no evidence to show what he did or ate after his discharge.

label: text
text: The jury returned a verdict of death from coal gas poisoning adding that no blame or negligence was attached to anyone. They added a rider that in such cases gas masks should be used, the wearing of them to be supervised by a competent Chinese foreman.
